1. Executive Summary
Overview
Increasing the supply of high-quality information from independent, credible sources and
building societal resilience to mis-, dis-, and mal-information (MDM) is a global priority. In
response, USAID and its Implementing Partners (IPs) have developed and implemented a wide
range of activities designed to mitigate the harms associated with manipulated information
across global regions and sectors, including but not limited to Democracy, Human Rights, and
Governance (DRG), Health, and the Office of Transitional Initiatives (OTI).
This Program Review provides an overview of the breadth and depth of USAID's programming
related to Information Resilience and Integrity (IRI). It is based on a detailed examination of 23
projects that cover all regions where USAID operates and a wide range of activity types,
including "supply-side" interventions focusing on media development, regulatory reform, content
creation, and others - along with "demand-side" interventions that aim to help citizens detect
and critically respond to non-credible information sources, attenuate the influence of content
from malign actors, and achieve related goals.
This Program Review is not an evaluation of USAID's IRI portfolio. Rather, it aims to understand
the types of interventions being funded by USAID; identify gaps in programming; provide an
updated typology that reflects the scope of USAID's IRI programing; examine strategies for
monitoring, evaluations, learning, and research (MERL); and provide a summary of the
emerging evidence on what's working. Based on the findings, the Program Review offers a set
of recommendations to USAID related to programming and MERL strategies. A full description
of the goals and research questions is provided below.
This review draws on two principal information sources. First, the research team carried out a
document review for 23 programs, based on project descriptions, quarterly and annual reports,
M&E plans, evaluations, and other relevant materials provided by USAID and IPs. Second, the
team conducted 20 Key Informant Interviews (Klls) with 41 individuals, including USAID HQ and
Mission personnel, as well as IP staff based in the US and in country offices. In collaboration
with USAID, the study team selected seven countries for in-depth case studies, reflecting the
diversity of contexts and project types that fall under USAID's information resilience and integrity
portfolio. In each case study country, the research team interviewed Mission personnel and in-
country staff from implementing partners.'
Key Findings
1. USAID programming related to information resilience and integrity includes a diverse
set of projects with distinct objectives and theories of change. While the wide set of
activities are all conceptually related, respondents consulted for this report noted some

3. While there is widespread support for addressing cross-cutting issues related to
gender and marginalized / vulnerable groups, few projects make this a central goal,
and respondents disagreed about whether targeted programming was always needed.
Respondents expressed support for the general idea that USAID and IPs should do more to
address MDM related to gender and marginalized groups, which can increase the risks of
violence against these groups and discourage participation in politics, among other harms.
Respondents agreed that these issues were often not being adequately considered during
program design. Consistent with this, the program review found that only eight of 23
projects incorporated cross-cutting issues in meaningful ways. However, views on the
importance of program targeting differed among respondents. While many expressed
support for activities designed to address group-specific harms related to MDM, other
respondents viewed interventions as taking a "whole-of-society" approach that benefited all
social segments, making targeting unnecessary.
4. Theories of change are typically not assessed by existing MERL approaches. The
theories of change articulated in project documents typically emphasize high-level impacts,
including increased availability of quality information, greater demand for impartial
information, increased citizen participation, improved inclusion and tolerance, and greater
transparency and accountability in government. MERL plans, on the other hand, tend to
focus mainly on outputs and short-term outcomes, including the number of journalists
trained and workshops held,the number of legal reforms attempted, the reach of content
8

produced by USAID-supported actors, and other related measures. The focus on outputs
and short-term outcomes reflects the inherent difficulties of measuring long-term outcomes
and impacts for most IRI projects. Moreover, in some cases it is neither desirable nor
feasible to focus on impacts, including in conflict-affected and transitioning countries, where
evolving political condition and project objectives may limit opportunities for measuring
impacts. In other cases, though, opportunities exist for integrating MERL approaches that
have the potential to narrow the gap between the goals expressed in TOCs and the data
collected to track program implementation and effectiveness.
5. There is an insufficient evidence base to allow for definitive conclusions about the
effectiveness of some IRI activities on higher-order outcomes. Impact evaluations
based on randomized-controlled trials and other credible research designs are rare for IRI
projects, and the existing academic literature is under-developed in this area. Despite this,
there is widespread agreement that some interventions - particularly those related to media
development and media literacy - can be effective at building the capacity of media
organizations and other stakeholders to provide accurate, independent information and
building skills citizens need to navigate complex information landscapes. Additional research
will be valuable for helping USAID and IPs more fully "tell the story" of program successes,
test intervention strategies, and examine the relative effectiveness of alternative
approaches.
Summary of Recommendations
Based on the key findings outlined here, as well as others described in subsequent sections, we
offer a set of recommendations related to programming and MERL approaches to USAID and
its partners. The recommendations are described in more detail at the end of the report.
Programmatic Recommendations
1. Expand programming informed by behavior change theory and designed for
adaptability, iteration, and learning.
2. Prioritize refining and expanding media literacy programs.
3. Consider expanding strategic communications programs related to information
resilience.
4. Consider ways of integrating non-media programming more fully in the information
resilience and counter-MDM toolkit.
5. Develop theories of change that match project timelines.
6. Reconsider how USAID approaches relationships with social media platforms in its
programming.
7. Encourage IPs to design programs with deeper consideration of gender equity and
social inclusion (GESI) issues
9

MERL Recommendations
1. USAID should dedicate more resources to MERL for IRI/MDM programs.
2. Programs should consider increased usage of complexity-aware MERL strategies.
3. USAID and IPs should track how programs affect women and people from
marginalized groups as part of routine project monitoring.
4. National opinion surveys are useful for tracking attitudes and behaviors but in most
cases should not be used for outcome indicators.
5. Content reach is not a strong outcome indicator and should be coupled with other
means of assessing audience impact, when possible.
6. USAID should increase the use of impact evaluation methods for some types of
projects.
2. Goals, Research Questions, and Methodology
Goals and Research Questions
The goal of this program review is to examine the portfolio of USAID-funded projects related to
information resilience and integrity. This review does not serve as an evaluation of USAID-
funded projects; rather, it aims to take stock of USAID programming, and examine theories of
change, approaches to cross-cutting issues, monitoring and evaluation strategies, and evidence
of effectiveness. The review is guided by a set of research questions (RQs) initially presented in
the Concept Note and subsequently refined with input from USAID after project launch:
(RQ1) Theories of Change. How do USAID projects define information resilience and
integrity and conceptualize the harms associated with MDM? What types of theories of
change (TOC) are being used by projects seeking to prevent or address these harms? Are
there ways to improve TOCs for USAID's activities?
(RQ2) Stocktaking of Activities. What approaches are USAID and its implementing
partners using to build information resilience and integrity and to counter MDM? How are
these related to the theories of change above? What is the appropriate typology for
information resilience and integrity projects and adjacent programs? Are there types of
activities that are over- or under-represented?
(RQ3) Stocktaking of Approaches Related to Cross-Cutting Issues. What share of
projects are addressing issues related to gender and marginalized groups (e.g., immigrants,
minorities, LGBTQ communities, etc.)? What strategies are being used?
10

(RQ4) Stocktaking of MERL Approaches. What MERL strategies (and indicators) are
currently being used by USAID and its implementing partners? Are TOCs being used to
inform MERL strategies?
(RQ5) Analysis of Impact. Which of the current approaches seem to be working best to
increase information resilience and integrity and to address MDM? Which of the current
approaches have the most evidence to support their effectiveness? What contextual factors
affect the impact of these approaches?
(RQ6) Recommendations. Which approaches appear to be most promising? What
approaches are missing in USAID's current programs? What indicators should USAID use to
track program effectiveness? What additional MERL approaches should be considered?
Methodology
Document review. The study team compiled and examined program documents provided by
USAID related to 23 projects, including several that are regional in scope (see Annex D for a
list). Documents included: (1) program work plans; (2) quarterly and annual reports; (3) MERL
plans; and (4) and evaluation/research reports (see Annex H for a complete list of documents).
Based on this material, the team catalogued activities by type, refined the typology of USAID
information resilience and integrity programming, and analyzed information related to the core
research questions, focusing on theories of change, MERL strategies, cross-cutting issues, and
evidence of impact.
Key Informant Interviews (Klls). The study team conducted 20 Klls with a total of 41
participants. This included interviews with headquarters personnel from USAID and
Implementing Partners. The team also conducted interviews with USAID Mission staff and IPs in
six case study countries: Ukraine, Georgia, Serbia, Libya, Nicaragua, and Indonesia.? The Klls
for the case studies were designed to complement information obtained through the document
review and allow for further exploration of core topics. The set of case study countries was
chosen in collaboration with USAID to ensure the inclusion of multiple project types and
implementing partners, and to cover multiple regions and political regime types. The study team
conducted all Klls remotely between May 12 and July 14, 2023.

3. Theories of Change
RQ1.1: How do USAID projects define information resilience and integrity and
conceptualize the harms associated with MDM?
Primary Findings:
• USAID staff largely pull from similar definitions of MDM and consider information
resilience a broader, longer-term goal than countering MDM.
• The harms attributed to MDM and low information resilience are many and varied,
producing several distinct families of change theories.
RQ1.2: What types of theories ofchange (TOC) arebeing used by projects seeking to
prevent or address these harms?
Primary Finding:
•
While USAID supports many IRI activities, programming is concentrated in two main
areas: media development and citizen engagement / literacy. Strict "counter-MDM"
activities are rare.
RQ1.3: Are there ways to improve TOCs for USAID's activities?
Primary Finding:
•
Theories of change shouldbe less abstract and more measurable, better connecting
proposed activities to desired changes, which were often high-level and vague.
Improving information resilience, promoting information integrity, and responding to MDM are
broad goals. The projects considered in this review tackled them in many different ways: some
attempt to improve the supply of quality media and public access to it. Others try to understand
and respond directly to low-integrity information from bad actors. Still others disseminate
alternative narratives meant to blunt the impact of MDM and promote social cohesion and other
goals.
This section of the report explores how programs describe what they aim to achieve, and how
they hope to achieve it. It explores competing conceptions of the core problem, examines the
types of harms programs are concerned with, and summarizes common interventions used to
prevent or mitigate those harms. Some theories of change operate purely on a systemic level
such as national media environments, while others are focused on specific changes in
behaviors or (more rarely) attitudes.
Not every program provided documents explicitly laying out a theory of change, and even fewer
used the classic "if-then," format. For those projects that did not, this review tries to infer one
from stated objectives or other available information. Sometimes, interviews were the best way
12

of assessing a given program's theory of change. Most projects focused on media development,
support for journalists and media outlets, or various forms of media literacy. Other theories of
change were less well-represented.
In general, even theories of change that were explicitly spelled out in program documents
sometimes contained gaps, leaps of logic, or vagaries that inhibit monitoring and evaluation.
This often leads to disconnects between theories of change and MERL indicators. These issues
are elaborated on in later sections that take stock of activities and MERL approaches.
Defining the Problem
The goals of promoting high-integrity information and a resilient media environment are distinct
from countering MDM. This distinction was an important theme during interviews. Which of
these frames a program uses often informs its theory of changeas does the way it articulates
the associated harms.
The Executive Branchhas already weighed in on this distinction and provided a starting point
for common definitions of a wider frame. In a December 2022 "Roadmap for Researchers on
Priorities Related to Information Integrity Research and Development,"the National Science &
Technology Council laid out four goals:3
- to help individuals discern between "high-integrity" and "low-integrity" information,
- to prevent or minimize avoidable harms from information manipulation,
- to promote resiliencethe ability of people to operate in the context of potentially
questionable information and of communities to "maintain appropriate levels of
information integrity" despite uncertainty or active manipulations,
- and the collection of "high-quality evidence" for evaluating strategies for addressing
information integrity challenges.
This suggests that at high levels within the US government, a distinction is being made between
two terms that were often used but not well-defined during interviews for this project:
"information integrity" and "information resilience." The

The goals of promoting high-integrity information and a resilient media environment are distinct
from countering MDM (or "low-integrity information"). This distinction was an important theme
during interviews. Which of these frames a program uses often informs its theory of changeas
does the way it articulates the associated harms.
Many interview participants referenced "Mis-, Dis-, and Mal-information" as challenges to
information integrity and resilience. This specific combination of terms reflects that USAID staff
largely draw on the conceptual framework laid out by Claire Wardle's work on "Information
Disorder." When asked, all of the USAID staff interviewed for this report defined these terms as
Wardle does: misinformation is the incidental, unintentional spread of false or misleading
information—essentially rumors—while disinformation is understood to be intentional. (Mal-
information is used less commonly and refers to true information used intentionally to harm,
such as the release of hacked materials.) Many interviewees referenced Wardle and her work
directly by name.
Some interview participants also felt that the definitions on offer, while widely cited, lacked a
necessary degree of clarity around nuanced and sometimes sensitive issues. Some felt that
"countering MDM" evokes geopolitical aspects of strategic communications by external
authoritarian governments, even in contexts where domestic sources of MDM were more
influential and harmful. Several expressed an appetite for more precise termseven MDM
obscures important differences between mis-and disinformation, for instance.
Interviewees typically agreed that resilience is a longer-term,
broader goal than countering MDM. A few said that countering
MDM was more "reactive" than promoting IRI. Some took a
societal perspective and distinguished between efforts to
expose and hold bad actors accountable and efforts to create
a resilient environment in which those actors are less harmful.
Others took a more individual-level perspective, seeking to
identify and reduce harmful "end-state behaviors" motivated
by MDM.

The Klls revealed that there is considerable variation in whether and how USAID and IP

A smaller number of programs focused on producing attitudinal changes, rather than behavioral
changes. For example, the Georgia Information Integrity Project (GIIP), seeks to promote
solidarity within Georgia and weaken disinformation narratives targeting the anxieties about
Georgia's relationship with Europe and NATO through strategic communications. An example
was the "Fruits of Heroism" campaign it developed in conjunction with Georgian partners for
audiences in rural communities near the contested border with Russia. Individuals associated
with this program said that communities in those areas often feel cut off, neglected by Tbilisi,
and vulnerable to Russian hostility; this campaign recast them as patriotic heroes on the front
line and encouraged Georgians in the capital to consume produce from those regions.
Categorizing Theories of Change
This review groups the theories of change pursued by USAID programs into five categories. By
far the two largest are programs aiming to improve citizen engagement with media and those
working to support national media sectors through systemic reform and increased capacity in
individual organizations. A smaller set of programs focus on connecting and augmenting the
work of other stakeholders, on monitoring and understanding MDM and its sources, and on
responding to MDM through strategic communications offering alternative narratives.
1. Citizen engagement with information. Projects in this area tend to center the well-informed
citizen as a necessary component of democracy. These programs often work to provide "neutral
information" to audiences so they can, for example, make informed decisions during elections.
16

They might also seek to mitigate harms like voter suppression through disinformation. Many
programs focus on developing some element of media literacy. Media literacy is understood in
many different ways, and programs under the media literacy umbrella include those aiming to
educate citizens about the media ecosystem, raise awareness of MDM, or help citizens identify
and avoid sharing rumors and propaganda.
Examples of the types of theories of change being used in this area include the following:
• IF critical thinking skills and media information literacy among citizens are
strengthened...THEN citizens will use more accurate, objective news and information in
their decision-making. (Azerbaijan Media and Journalism Activity)
• IF public demand for quality journalism grows...THEN the civically relevant role of media will
be strengthened, and citizens will be equipped with quality information that counters malign
influence and supports European integration. (Media Program in Ukraine)
• IF youth gain and apply media literacy and critical thinking skills as part of their education
and in other youth-friendly formats....and IF they demand and drive increased volume of
high-quality, fact-based, and relevant professional media content, THEN youth will be able
to not only navigate but also shape an information ecosystem that informs and engages as
opposed to divides and polarizes, resulting in increased resilience to disinformation and
efforts to undermine democracy. (North Macedonia, YouThink)
2. Systemic and organizational support to media. Programs sometimes draw an explicit link
between audience demand for high quality content—driven by their ability to recognize and
access it-and the increased supply of that content, driven by audience growth and other forms
of support to both the media sector, individual outlets, and related civil society groups.
Many programs centered their theory of change on this support, which can include training for
journalists, legal and technological support, grants to modernize newsroom business practices,
provision of new infrastructure or equipment, advocacy for legal and regulatory reforms affecting
the enabling environment for media, and support for independent high-quality content, among
other things. Interviewed individuals were quick to point out that much of this is "traditional
media activity" supported by USAID, which can be effective for reason beyond contributing to
IRI. For example, some projects mentioned the watchdog role of media, while others
emphasized that only professional, credible media can establish the bonds of trust with
audiences necessary to inform the public. Some stressed that to survive and reach their full
potential, media needs to make significant improvements to its business operations.

increase capacity of local partners through hubs dedicated to research, training, and co-creation

Media Organizational & Systemic Support (17 out of 23 programs). These programs include
efforts to support media at the environmental and operational levels—for example by supporting
media reforms, improving the business environment for news media, providing legal or security
assistance to journalists, or directly supporting content production. Theories of Change under
this category tend to focus on increasing the "supply" of quality media. They may do this by
improving the legal, regulatory, and financial factors within the enabling environment for media,
or by improving the ability of individual media outlets to sustain themselves and create engaging
content.
The words organizational and systemic were chosen purposefully for this exercise. Many of the
programs in this review work to improve what is often called the "enabling environment" for
media outlets—factors like the legal and regulatory regime and business climate for media.
These programs help media as a system thrive. Other programs offer training, equipment,
audience research, funding for content, or other forms of capacity and support to individual
media partners. Some programs do both.
It is important to note that this report uses media in a broad sense, referring to any actor
providing information to the public. Civil Society organizations, for example, are not typically
classified as media—but when they produce content meant to be consumed as a supplement to
news and information, they are treated that way by this typology.

One interview participant asked that media infrastructure be included in any new typology. "One
of the types of programming we support is infrastructure, like supporting hard infrastructure
around radio access to hard-to-reach areas," they said. "This can be a theory of change of
access to reliable information. Access to life-saving information is a piece in and of itself, but it's
also a place where disinformation can be particularly harmful." The development of media
infrastructure should be included here.
Finally,this typology separates out efforts to hold social media platforms accountable for their
media effects into two distinct areas: the effects of their business models and content
recommendations on the media environment as a whole fall under this category. Efforts to
improve content moderation fall under a different category: understanding, exposing, and
reacting to MDM. It is noteworthy that none of the programs reviewed for this report focused on
the former type of platform accountability; it is included here to account for other projects which
may not have been included in this review. Future projects may also fall under this area.
Common output indicators in this category include:
• Journalists receiving training or assistance (security, legal, etc.)
• Number of individuals receiving media literacy training
• The reach of specific news outlets or content
Outcome indicators include:
• Improvements in media professionalism, business practices, and sustainability
• Post-training assessments on topics like conflict and gender sensitivity
• the number of outlets which implement recommended reforms,
• policy and regulatory changes (or defeat of proposed negative changes)
Many projects in this category have indicators strongly tied to media development outcomes,
but not every program ties its operational "output" indicators to outcomes this directly. For
example, many projects measure the number of journalists trained or supported, without
measuring changes in the impact that those journalists are able to make on the information
environment. Some of the best indicators of support are qualitative, like the passage of certain
reforms after an advocacy campaign. Causality can be difficult to quantitatively prove in these
cases, but it is still useful evidence of impact.
Improving Citizen Engagement with Media (10 out of 23 programs). This category includes
efforts to better equip citizens to navigate the information environment, identify credible news
sources, and distinguish them from untrustworthy sources. This often involves some form of
media literacy education—in schools, through adult training programs, or in other venues.
Sometimes education occurs online through social media campaigns or games designed to

impart media literacy skills or best practices. It also includes forms of content, like fact-checks,
designed to help individuals assess the veracity of claims. Many of these programs aim to
amplify their reach by providing training to educators or peer-to-peer trainers, who share

Theories of change in this category often emphasize the relationship between a robust media
and an informed citizenry capable of holding government actors accountablewhat one
program called a "vibrant, independent media sector capable of shaping democratic discourse."
They sometimes frame this as increasing "demand" for high quality content by helping citizens
recognize and access trustworthy journalism. The relationship between supply and demand
means there is significant overlap between Category ! (systemic and operational support for

Common indicators under this category include output measures like:
• Number of events or trainings held, and number of individuals trained
• Reach of online media literacy campaigns
• Participants who share skills from media literacy trainings with others
• Adoption of media literacy curricula in educational institutions
• Fact-checks or voter educational materials produced by the implementer or their
partners
Outcome indicators include:
• Number of individuals who show or self-report improved media literacy and (often
measured through surveys or post-training evaluations)
• Changes in media consumer behavior such as use of verification techniques or avoiding
biased sources

It can be difficult to draw a causal line connecting participation in media literacy interventions,

their most rigorous, MERL plans for projects in this category may conduct controlled trials to
establish a causal link between outputs like training and outcomes like improved literacy. More

Understanding, Exposing, and Reacting to MDM (8 out of 23 programs). This category
includes efforts to monitor disinformation, expose its sources, understand how it spreads, and
evaluate or pursue appropriate responses. Sometimes this activity takes the form of media-
monitoring; when fact-checking is used to inform programmatic or other responses in addition to
correcting claims for the public, it can also fit in this category. Likewise, efforts to foster platform
accountability fit in this category when they aim to identify social media content policy violations
and escalate them to companies for moderation. Because these activities take MDM and its
spread as their focus, they are considered to be "supply-side" activities looking to detect and
reduce low-integrity information.
Relatively few projects of the 23 projects reviewed for this report fell in this category. Only two of
them comprised activities other than "research," and their theories of change rarely hinged on
these activities. Rather, research and monitoring often support other programming goals, such
as capacity-building, media literacy training for election officials, or strategic communications.
There is a significant overlap between this category and Category V (information resilience
hubs); three of the four projects included in this category were also included in Category V. This
is probably a reflection of the fact that research findings are valuable to many organizations,
making it useful to embed research activities in network-building activities so findings can be
shared widely.

• Number of disinformation networks detected
• Number of misleading pieces of content fact-checked
• Number of partners who participated in creation of research plans
• Number of partners who use research tools developed by the project

might be considered both supply-and demand-focused because the content produced by
projects like this is meant (in part) to reduce demand for other, more harmful content.

• The number of trainings held for hub members
•Number of participants in training programs or co-creation activities

• Reach of co-created communications campaigns or trainings

"wicked" problems - posing significant challenges for developing appropriate MERL strategies.
Complex problems are those for which there are key knowledge gaps in the scientific evidence
about the problem and/or the solutions, and multiple stakeholders, each with different expertise
and knowledge gaps, are required to address the issue. Evidence-based decisions are often
difficult to make because of the gaps in knowledge. Wicked problems are those for which there
is minimal scientific evidence about the problem and/or the solutions, and multiple stakeholders,
often with conflicting values or interests, are required to address the issue. Making purely
evidence-based decisions is often impossible, due not only to the lack of evidence but also to
the lack of agreement among stakeholders. 10,11
Because of this complexity or wickedness, and because addressing IRI/MDM issues typically
requires changes to entire systems (e.g., media environments, social attitudes/cohesion), it can
be difficult or impossible to predict all the effects a program will have on society. Many programs
acknowledged this and integrated complexity-aware MEL approaches into their MEL plans to
monitor for emergent program outcomes and/or changes in context that would affect the
program's ability to meet their intended outcomes. CAMEL approaches used in the programs
we reviewed include outcome harvesting; the use of sentinel indicators to watch for changes in
context; developing and implementing learning agendas that cover complex aspects of a
program, like how to build audience trust; and conducting learning activities, such as Pause &
Reflect sessions.
Interview respondents noted several challenges in measuring the outcomes and impact of IRI
and countering MDM programs. Chief among these challenges is the fact that IRI/MDM take
place in complex, ever-changing contexts, and we have very limited knowledge about how
changes in the context affect program goals. Thus, it is difficult to assess the degree to which
observed outcomes and impacts can be attributed to the program.

Asking "what works" to improve IRI in the face of MDM challenges is much like asking "what
works" to address climate change—the truth is, no intervention or even suite of interventions
can solve the problem fully. The challenges MDM poses cannot be banished, but their worst
effects can be mitigated: media literacy can diminish the impact of low-integrity information;
media development can strengthen suppliers of trustworthy news; and strategic communication
can provide authoritative information and promote beneficial behaviors.
This essential combination of systemic adjustments and individual-level interventions is
reflected by the diversity of theories of change for projects included in this review. The
challenges of monitoring, evaluation, and learning enumerated above make it difficult to
definitively say "what works" for fostering IRI and countering MDM. Even the broader body of
academic literature is inconclusive on many key questions.2 Moreover, national context matters
greatly, which limits the generalizability of findings from one place to other contexts.

evidence to commend them than others. Other approaches, like fact-checking and working
directly with social media companies to improve content moderation, generally appear to work

Is Media Development a Counter-MDM Strategy?
Media development—the most common type of program reviewed for this report—has
significant achievements to tout. The Media Program in Ukraine, for example, has assisted
many local and regional media outlets in their transition from state-run media to publicly funded
media. Ukrainian Civil Society also successfully advocated for reforms to the Ukrainian national
public broadcaster and against proposed legislation that would have hampered media freedom.
In Serbia, the Strengthening Media Systems program tracks the revenue and audience growth
of small local outlets who transitioning from government and grant funding to more commercially
viable models of journalism, which have stymied their reach and innovation. In the Democratic
Republic of the Congo, radio stations that received USAID-supported trainings were rated as
more professional by their listeners.
But those achievements do little to answer a key follow-up question: does this work lessen the
impact of mis- and disinformation? It is noteworthy that of the five categories in the above
typology, support for media is the only category solely located in the "information resilience"
column-media literacy work, for example, spans both information resilience and harm
mitigation. The ultimate goal of media development programs may be something other than
mitigating harms from low-integrity information, such as strengthening the professionalism,
sustainability, accessibility, and independence of the media system and individual outlets.
These are worthwhile objectives but neither USAID nor other stakeholders can say for certain
they will go on to lessen the effects of MDM. Academic research suggests there is a relationship
between the health of independent mediaespecially local media—and factors like civic
participation, trust in institutions, belief in conspiracy theories, and political polarization. For

As with media development, strategic communications programs can benefit from a behavior
change lens in both their design and evaluation. The use of strategic communications to shift
behaviors and attitudes is a relatively novel area for USAID's media and democracy
programming: the GlIP, by far the most strategic communications-oriented program reviewed
here, was consistently described as novel, innovative, and distinct. But public health programs
have been thinking about the link between communications, attitudes, and behavior since at
least the AIDS crisis. The lessons learned by public health programs (and some counter-MDM
programs like the Madani initiative in Indonesia) during the COVID-19 pandemic offer promising
paths forward. Interviews revealed two key themes.
First, it is more straightforward to pursue and measure behavior change than to neutralize
propaganda. Interview participants from USAID's public health programs stressed that the
specifics of rumors and propaganda are a secondary concern: from their perspective, the
important outcome is health-conscious behaviors like handwashing or avoiding contact with
contagious individuals. Future media and strategic communications programming could benefit
from similar concrete goals.
The second theme is that high-integrity information and media literacy alone cannot overcome
the social determinants of behavior and belief; for that, programs need approaches that take the
social dimension into account. An example comes from the 2014 Ebola outbreak, when rumors
claimed that the bodies of deceased patients were being used for organ harvesting—a false
claims that, in the words of an interviewee "get into the sacred." As a result, fewer individuals
reported deaths of loved ones from Ebola, greatly increasing the risk of transmission as they
chose to handle human remains themselves. USAID partners combatted these rumors directly
by switching from black body bags to clear ones and even making the walls of some medical
facilities transparent. People could confirm for themselves that no organ harvesting occurred.
Without this verification, individuals were unwilling to trust official reassurances about the
handling of their loved ones' remains.
Responses to MDM can do more than consider social dynamics—they can also incorporate and
benefit from them. In an interview with USAID's public health team, the said that during the
COVID-19 pandemic they noticed that a major determinant of whether or not an individual took
up key behaviors was how they were received by their community: even highly educated
individuals often became skeptical of health authorities if surrounded by friends and family who
behaved similarly. For this reason, programs began working more closely with prominent local
community figures like faith leaders to disseminate health information. A priest may not be more
knowledgeable about medicine than a doctor, but they are probably more influential within their
parish.

As noted, projects designed to improve citizen engagement with media were the second most

8. Recommendations
Programmatic Recommendations
1. Expand programming informed by behavior change theory and designed for
adaptability, iteration, and learning. USAID's Office of Transitions Initiatives runs projects on
significantly shorter timeframes than most USAID teams; their timelines are measured in
months, not years, and include frequent pauses to reflect, assess, learn, and adapt. This
iterative process treats research and practice as a loop in which each component continually
informs and supports the other. It is essential to OTI's work because of the crisis and conflict
contexts in which OTI typically does programming. USAID programs run by other teams could
benefit from this approach.
This is especially true for programs whose ultimate objective either includes or implies some
form of behavior change (as well as, but much less commonly, attitudinal change). Many
programs—especially those related to media development, media literacy, and strategic
communications—focus on the relationship between the supply of and demand for quality
43

information. These programs typically believe an informed citizenry is desirable for a
reason—that informed citizens will be less susceptible to propaganda, act to hold governments
accountable, be more engaged politically, be more tolerant of their neighbors, be less prone to
violence, or some other outcome.
This change in behavior is often the ultimate aim of a program, but it is often left unmeasured. A
program might for example measure whether citizens who received media literacy training
changed the sources of media they consume; but few go on to assess whether or not this
changed their daily behavior and attitudes in ways that benefit social cohesion and democratic
governance.
Efforts to inform, educate, and communicate with the public should not only be evaluated on
consumption of information or knowledge gained from training—they should also measure
whether or not those outcomes affected ultimate behavioral objectives. Some programs
measure this through outcome harvesting, focus groups, or other forms of qualitative research.
These are valid learning opportunities but could be combined with RCTs and other experimental
approaches for even greater insights about whether the selected intervention drove the desired
change. It may be, for example, that citizens do consume more credible sources of information
after training but do little else to further democratic governance owing to social factors (e.g. their
friends and family still hold certain beliefs, leading to peer pressure), economic factors (e.g. they
remain unable to participate politically because of financial obstacles), or political factors (e.g.
credible news coverage does not change their political apathy or sense of powerlessness).
These would be important insights for overcoming barriers to change, and programs should be
designed to collect and account for them.
2. Prioritize refining and expanding media literacy programs. Both USAID MERL data and
academic literature suggest that media literacy can be effective if approached in specific ways.
This is an ongoing area of research and USAID should assess the effectiveness of media
literacy programs more deeply and iteratively, in keeping with recommendation 1 above.
Unfortunately, few USAID programs are set up to assess whether the provision of media literacy
education leads to enduring changes in behavior like verifying source credibility or avoiding
untrustworthy outlets. Some programs, like the Media Program in Ukraine (SBU), attempt to
measure this through national surveys-but these are a poor instrument because changes
cannot be causally attributed to programs (see MERL Recommendation 6). The SBU
acknowledged as much in a mid-term evaluation:
In order to independently verify whether ML efforts actually increased citizens' abilities to
determine quality information and to consume more high-quality content, it would be
necessary to study citizens who have been reached by MPU ML activities, rather than
the journalism professionals who were interviewed or surveyed for this evaluation. Even
in a mass survey, the issue of the link between ML efforts and any changes in the mass
data would be elusive without an experimental setup comparing control and treatment
groups.
44

Likewise, in Indonesia, the Advancing Media Literacy for New Digital Arrivals in Developing
Countries' (AML's) FY22 first quarterly progress report reached similarly conclusions: Moonshot,
one of the implementing partners, wrote that it is planning a "series of experiments" on media
literacy to "establish a more accurate measurement for behavioral and attitudinal change."
In keeping with recommendation 1 above, media literacy programs should be evaluated not just
on national surveys or post-training test scores but also on whether the conveyed skills make a
difference in the daily lives of citizens and their communities. This can be more difficult to
measure but is ultimately more important. It is also important to avoid self-assessments as a
metric for media and information literacy. Research has also shown individuals to be susceptible
to the Dunning Kreuger effect when evaluating their own ability to navigate the media
environment—that is to say, many individuals are overconfident in their level of literacy."
3. Consider expanding strategic communications programs related to information
resilience. The strategic communications campaigns under GIIP are among the more
innovative activities reviewed for this report. Disinformation often involves narratives, beliefs,
and social divisions that are subjective and non-falsifiable; alternative narratives are an
appropriate way of addressing these issues. For example, the GIIP program attempted to create
economic links between Tbilisi and regions of Georgia that felt economically isolated and
exposed to a hostile Russia-addressing the sort of social divisions and economic inequities
that make societies vulnerable to disinformation in the first place. They are also amenable to the
kinds of flexible, iterative implementation and learning approaches advocated for in
recommendation 1.
Despite the promise of strategic communications, the GIIP was one of only two programs
categorized as strategic communications by this review. While USAID teams working in public
health and conflict resolution often use strategic communications and counter-messaging
programs in their work, this review found some hesitance to do so for IRI programs. In an
interview, one USAID staffer involved with the GlIP said it could be characterized as promoting
attitudinal change; they expected,but to date have not heard, concerns that it is out of scope for
USAID and more befitting a State Department public diplomacy program. Some DRG
implementing partners also described discomfort with the notion of pursing behavior and
attitudinal change in their work.
USAID should pause to consider whether and how it wants to proceed with this area of
programming, which carries both promise and risk. In an interview, one USAID staffer also
expressed concerns that "counternarratives" are not effective, raising the possibility that to
justify investments in strategic communications programs, "alternative narratives" must be
sufficiently distinct from attempts to merely present USG perspectives more assertively in the
face of adversarial propaganda.

macro-social goals like more accountable government, social stability, or resilience against
attempts to undermine democracy - outcomes that typically cannot be realized on a five-year
cycle. Theories of change should include a series of more modest discrete steps that can be
achieved and measured in the allotted timeframe. It may be the case that the ultimate objective
is still generational change, and programs may even stipulate this in writingbut they should
make clear how each iteration of a five-year program will incrementally contribute toward the
envisioned end goal.
6. Reconsider how USAID approaches relationships with social media platforms in its
programming. As mentioned above, few programs in this review explicitly worked either with
social media platforms to improve content moderation or with civil society advocates to improve
regulation of social media companies. What evidence did surface during this review suggests
that the latter—a focus on regulating social media's financial and editorial impact on media as
part of the wider enabling environment—is more promising. Even before widespread layoffs in
the tech sector depleted trust and safety teams, the USAID programs in this review struggled to
interface effectively with platforms. USAID should examine potential strategies beyond
engagement on content moderation.
7. Encourage IPs to design programs with deeper consideration of gender equity and
social inclusion (GESI) issues. From the documents we reviewed, we found that only about a
third of all programs had meaningfully incorporated GESI considerations in program designs.
Another third of the programs addressed GESI issues but in a cursory way. When planning
programs, IPs should think beyond ensuring that women and people from marginalized groups
benefit from their programs. They should also think about 1) whether/how issues of IRI/MDM
and their programs impact women and people from marginalized groups differently than men
and people from non-marginalized groups and 2) how to make the positive impacts on women
and people from marginalized groups sustainable. For example, instead of addressing GESI
solely by ensuring that a certain percentage of the journalists trained are women, media
development programs can train journalists to have a GESI lens when reporting on major
issues. They can also help media organizations and government institutions develop and
implement GESI policies that promote equal opportunities for women and people from
46

marginalized groups—activities that will likely produce sustainable results and have a greater
long-term impact on women and people from marginalized groups. Similarly, media literacy
programs can acknowledge that, although many people may be exposed to the same MDM, the
messages may affect non-marginalized men differently than women and people from
marginalized groups. Using this knowledge, these programs can include in their trainings
information on how MDM is often targeted to certain groups and against other groups to disturb
social cohesion.
MERL Recommendations
1. USAID should dedicate more resources to MERL for IRI/MDM programs. The biggest
modifiable challenge related to assessing the impact of programs was a lack of resources,
including budget, time, and staff. USAID should prioritize funding of MERL, dedicating a
minimum of 5% of each program's budget to monitoring, internal evaluation, and learning. In
addition, USAID should plan to set aside funding for external evaluations, including impact
evaluations, for a subset of high-priority programs that are amenable to this type of evaluation
(see recommendation 6 below). Beyond funding, USAID should also recognize the time
required to design and implement high-quality MERL plans and allow programs more flexibility
for program learning and adaptation. Finally, USAID can encourage IPs to update theories of
change and results frameworks as they adapt their programming.
2. Programs should consider increased usage of complexity-aware MERL strategies.
Programs facing high uncertainty that aim to quickly test interventions, adapt, and iterate, can
benefit from MERL systems that can adapt with the program. This means reducing the size and
burden of their theory-based MERL systems (results framework, indicators, etc.) to allow time
and resources for complexity-aware and flexible approaches.
Often when thinking about complexity-aware approaches to MERL, people think about data
collection methods, like outcome harvesting or most significant change. Although these
methods can be used in complexity-aware ways, CAMEL is first and foremost a set of principles
that guide the way programs use MERL. These principles include:
1. Attend to the blind spots of program theory-based monitoring and evaluation. Identify
and assess uncertain and unpredictable cause and effect relationships in the project
logic model.
2. Monitor systemically (interrelationships, perspectives, and boundaries).
3. Synchronize MEL with the pace of change.
CAMEL is particularly appropriate when:
• There are uncertain and unpredictable cause and effect relationships in the project logio
model.
• A project is subject to influence by contextual factors.
• A project is likely to contribute to emergent (unpredictable) outcomes.
47

• Stakeholders bring diverse perspectives; goals and strategies are contested; and
consensus is impractical.
• The pace of change is dynamic, and changes in the context lead to new opportunities
and/or needs.
• Adaptive management is necessary to effectively implement a program.
Programs will always have limited resources and will need to prioritize what they monitor. Most
programs will have some parts of the program that are particularly sensitive to complexity and
others that are not. When prioritizing what and how to monitor, USAID and IPs should use
CAMEL approaches to monitor the aspects of the program that are sensitive to complexity and
theory-based MERL approaches (e.g., indicators) to monitor the parts of the program were
uncertainty is lower.
3. USAID and IPs should track how programs affect women and people from
marginalized groups as part of routine project monitoring. Many current programs' only
monitoring of their GESI impact is a disaggregation of the numbers of people served, usually by
gender but sometimes by other marginalized groups. Some programs also assess GESI impact
in their external end-of-program evaluations, but often there is little data available for external
evaluators. Programs should do more to monitor their GESI impact throughout the project life
cycle with a combination of indicator data and qualitative data. For indicators, programs should
consider disaggregating their outcome and output indicators by gender and any other targeted
marginalized groups. For example, in addition to disaggregating an output indicator on "number
of people trained," training programs can also disaggregate an outcome indicator on "percent of
trainees who demonstrated increased knowledge after the training." Programs can also
disaggregate average post-test training scores and training satisfaction surveys by
gender/marginalized groups and analyze results (e.g., with a question analysis) to see if there
are aspects of the training that are understood/appreciated differently by different groups. These
learnings, along with program staff observations and conversations had with training
participants, can then be used to improve the training and/or identify other types of interventions
that may be needed to better support women and marginalized groups. As another example,
programs that have output indicators related to the "number of people reached" can, to the
extent possible, disaggregate the numbers reached by gender or marginalized community,
based on social media profiles. Furthermore, they can conduct content analysis on comments to
see 1) if women and marginalized groups tend to have different responses than non-
marginalized men, and 2) whether any comments are about women or marginalized
communities and if so, what kinds of attitudes are represented in those comments.
4. National opinion surveys are useful for tracking attitudes and behaviors but in most
cases should not be used for outcome indicators. USAID projects often include measures
based on national public opinion surveys as part of the larger set of indicators included in M&E
plans, typically to measure media consumption habits, specific beliefs, or media literacy skills.
National opinion surveys are valuable for understanding baseline attitudes and behaviors and
tracking their evolution over time. For this reason, it may be valuable to conduct such surveys at
the start of projects and throughout their lifespan. However, survey-based measures are
48

typically not appropriate for use as outcome indicators and in most cases should not be used for
that purpose.
There are at least three challenges related to survey-based outcome indicators. First, even the
most successful projects generally produce small marginal changes in attitudes and behaviors
that may be too small to be detected in nationally-representative surveys of 1,000 to 1,200
respondents (the typical sample size for many surveys). Small changes (positive or negative) in
self-reported attitudes and behaviors from one survey to the next are likely to be attributable to
random variation between survey samples, rather than statistically-significant shifts. Second,
survey-based measures are subject to response biases that may be difficult to detect. For
example, short-term changes in self-reported media consumption data could reflect shifting
perceptions about the social desirability of "admitting" which media sources respondents
consume. Also, shifting contextual factors can affect self-assessments of media literacy skills,
as noted in Klls with respondents in Serbia. Third, and most important, it is typically not possible
to isolate the effect of USAID-funded projects on national-level measures of attitudes and
behaviors from surveys. Doing so requires identifying and accounting for the myriad other
factors that influence these measures, which is usually not possible. Due to this attribution
problem, USAID should discourage IPs from using survey-based measures as outcome
indicators.
5. Content reach is not a strong outcome indicator and should be coupled with other
means of assessing audience impact, when possible. Many programs use indicators of
audience reach as evidence that media content supported by a program was effective. This
might be true if the goal of a program is simple to expand the audience (and perhaps the
advertising or subscriber base) of an outlet or set of outlets. However, it says very little about
audience reaction to or uptake of messages included in that content—and for some programs
like media literacy or strategic communications, uptake and impact of the content on the
consumer is all-important. Reach can also be somewhat beside the point: content with high
reach could potentially backfire, for example, while content with lower reach might have
important effects in specific communities.
To complement indicators that measure reach, programs should consider both qualitative and
quantitative approaches that track impact. During the Kll interviews, Mission and IP staff
indicated that they sometimes use qualitative assessments to determine how content is
received. For example, many programs use focus groups, while the GIIP also conducts
sentiment analysis of the comments under social media posts. Additionally, experimental
approaches - including survey experiments and randomized-controlled trials - may be useful in
some contexts to document the impact of content on citizen attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors, as
described in recommendation 6.
6. USAID should increase the use of impact evaluation methods for some types of
projects. Impact evaluations based on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold
standard for evaluating program impacts. RCTs have several well-known limitations: they are
costly and time consuming; they are not appropriate for some types of projects and contexts;
they are difficult to implement and sometimes fail due to non-compliance with the randomization
49

protocol; and they sometimes do not produce actionable insights. Despite these limitations, it is
critical to include RCTs as part of a broad set of M&E strategies for learning about what works
(and what doesn't) in building resilient information ecosystems. However, in our document
review, we identified only a single RCT-based evaluation in the 23 programs examined (for a
journalist training activity in Tanzania'®). Building a stronger evidence base will require
selectively identifying opportunities for adopting RCTs as part of the broad suite of monitoring
and evaluation strategies. We stress that RCTs should complement, not replace, routine
monitoring and performance evaluation strategies that are critical for tracking project
implementation and learning lessons through other data collection methods, including those
described in recommendations 1 and 5.
RCTs are most useful and appropriate for interventions that meet three criteria. First, the activity
type is being (or has the potential to be) implemented in multiple countries. For projects that are
specific to a small number of countries or distinct contexts, there is generally less value in
conducting RCT-based evaluations since the results will not have relevance to a large set of
countries. Second, the intervention must be amenable to a randomized implementation
approach that creates control and treatment groups.' Some types of projects are not
appropriate because there are not enough participants to allow for this division and/or it would
be contrary to program goals to exclude some individuals or organizations in order to create a
control group. Third, RCTs are most useful when there is a limited or mixed evidence base for
an intervention, either because there is a lack of prior research, previous findings are mixed, or
there is considerable skepticism about its efficacy within USAID or IPs.
In our assessment, all USAID-funded activities included in this review have widespread usages
(or potential usage) and would be amenable to an RCT-based approach (at least for some
project components). Table 2 identifies the four interventions that meet the other two criteria,
making them most suitable for RCT-based impact evaluations. First, projects that provide
support for independent high-quality content frequently include a journalist training component
with a large number of participants, potentially allowing for a randomized implementation plan.
Moreover, the Tanzania RCT-based study mentioned above found that the training program had
no measurable effect on key outcomes, suggesting a need for additional research. Second,
while platform accountability projects are less commonplace, it is conceivable that they will be
implemented in an increasing number of countries over time. A recent literature review of MDM
interventions found that few studies have examined strategies for altering, labeling, or removing
social media content.2 Third, the literature review found limited evidence that media literacy
projects produce durable shifts in skills or behaviors in the Global South. Fourth, we are
unaware of any RCT-based research on alternative narratives.
